title: The first 90 seconds: what interviewers decide before you finish your intro
excerpt: First impressions form fast. Here's what interviewers notice early, and a simple plan for the opening minute and a half.
author: StarOrigin Editorial

seo.title: The first 90 seconds: what interviewers decide before you finish your intro
seo.description: Many hiring managers say they form a view within 90 seconds. What interviewers notice first, the common early disqualifiers, and a practical plan for your opening.

headline.title: The first 90 seconds:
headline.highlight: what interviewers decide before you finish your intro

lead: An interview may be booked for the best part of an hour, but impressions start forming before you've answered a single real question. Here's what gets noticed — and how to prepare for it.
intro:
Most candidates prepare hard for the difficult questions in the middle of an interview: the technical deep-dive, the conflict story, the salary conversation. Far fewer prepare for the moment that often shapes how those answers are heard — walking in, saying hello and introducing yourself.

That's not because interviewers are superficial. It's because people form impressions quickly, and then — usually without meaning to — look for evidence that confirms them. A strong opening buys you a fair hearing. A shaky one means the rest of the interview has to work harder.

sections.heading: What the numbers say
sections.html:
Industry surveys of hiring managers have repeatedly found that first impressions form fast:

  • About a third (33%) of hiring managers say they know whether they'll hire someone within the first 90 seconds.
  • The average interview lasts around 40 minutes — so that judgement can land in the first few percent of the conversation.
  • Before you even get to the room, recruiters typically scan a resume for just 5–7 seconds on a first pass.

Treat these as directional rather than precise — survey methods vary, and plenty of interviewers change their minds. But the pattern is consistent: the opening matters out of proportion to its length.

You don't have to win the interview in 90 seconds. You just have to avoid losing it there.

sections.heading: The early disqualifiers
sections.html:
The same industry surveys asked hiring managers which non-verbal mistakes most often count against a candidate. The list is striking because almost none of it is about competence:

MistakeHiring managers who cite it
Failure to make eye contact67%
Not knowing anything about the company47%
Lack of confidence or not smiling38%
Bad posture33%
Weak handshake26%
Crossed arms21%

Source: aggregated industry surveys of hiring managers; figures are indicative. The good news is that every item on this list is fixable with a little preparation.

sections.heading: A plan for your first 90 seconds
sections.html:
Before you arrive (or log in)

  • Know the company in three sentences: what it sells, who it sells to, and one recent development — a launch, an expansion, a new office. That alone answers the second-most-common complaint in the table above.
  • Arrive early, not too early. Ten minutes for in-person, two to three minutes for video. Rushing in flustered undoes everything else.
  • For video calls, test your camera, microphone and lighting beforehand. Put the camera at eye level and the interviewer's window just beneath it, so looking at them looks like eye contact.

The greeting (0–15 seconds)

  • Stand up straight, smile and make eye contact as you say hello.
  • Offer a firm, brief handshake where it's culturally appropriate — and follow the interviewer's lead if it isn't.
  • Use their name once: "Good to meet you, Priya." It signals attention without sounding rehearsed.

The small talk (15–45 seconds)

Interviewers often open with something easy — the commute, the weather, finding the building. Answer warmly and briefly, and hand the conversation back. This is a test of ease, not content.

The introduction (45–90 seconds)

"Tell me about yourself" is the question most people under-prepare for. Aim for roughly 60 seconds, structured as:

  1. Present: your current role and the one thing you're best known for.
  2. Past: one or two experiences that explain how you got here.
  3. Future: why this role, at this company, is the logical next step.
Try this: record your 60-second introduction on your phone, then watch it with the sound off. Are you making eye contact with the camera? Are your shoulders open? Do you look like you want to be there? Fix what you see, then record it again.

sections.heading: Body language without the acting
sections.html:
Advice about posture and gestures can make people stiff. The goal isn't to perform confidence — it's to remove the signals that get misread as disinterest or nerves:

  • Sit slightly forward, with both feet on the floor. It reads as engaged.
  • Keep your hands visible and relaxed on the table or in your lap. Crossed arms are often just comfortable, but many interviewers read them as defensive.
  • Pause before answering a hard question. A two-second pause looks thoughtful; a rushed answer looks anxious.
  • Mirror the energy in the room. A formal panel and a relaxed startup founder call for different tones.

sections.heading: If the start goes wrong
sections.html: Late because of traffic, tongue-tied on the intro, camera froze? It happens to everyone. Acknowledge it briefly, apologise once, and move on: "Sorry — let me start that again." Interviewers remember how you recover far more than the stumble itself. Then make the rest of the conversation count: specific examples, clear outcomes and good questions at the end.

sections.heading: Your pre-interview checklist
sections.html:
• Three-sentence summary of the company, plus one recent development.
  • A rehearsed 60-second introduction (present, past, future).
  • Two or three questions to ask the interviewer.
  • Route, timing and — for video — camera, audio and lighting tested.
  • A resume whose top third makes sense in five seconds.
